scenes.heading: DAGs
scenes.narration: A DAG, or directed acyclic graph, models a workflow as tasks connected by dependencies that never loop back.

scenes.heading: Why the DAG shape matters
bullets: Acyclic means no task depends on itself.
Independent branches can run in parallel.
The graph makes execution order unambiguous.
scenes.narration: The directed edges tell the engine which task must finish before another can start. Being acyclic guarantees the workflow always terminates, since no chain of dependencies loops. Branches that do not depend on each other run in parallel, and the graph leaves no doubt about the order of execution.

scenes.heading: Reading a DAG
scenes.narration: Execution starts at root tasks that have no dependencies. Downstream tasks wait until their upstream tasks succeed, and independent branches fan out to run at once. Where paths converge, a join task waits for all its upstreams before proceeding.

scenes.heading: Expressing dependencies
scenes.code:
extract >> [transform_a, transform_b] >> load

# equivalent explicit form:
# extract.set_downstream(transform_a)
# extract.set_downstream(transform_b)
# transform_a.set_downstream(load)
# transform_b.set_downstream(load)
scenes.narration: This one line says extract must finish before both transforms, which can then run in parallel. The load task waits until both transforms complete before it starts. The shift operator is just a readable shorthand for the explicit set_downstream calls shown below it.

scenes.text: A DAG encodes task order and parallelism without cycles, making complex workflows deterministic and easy to reason about.
scenes.narration: The acyclic guarantee is what ensures your workflow always finishes, because dependencies can never chase their own tail.
